milestones.name: A Mac program, a Chrome page and an iPhone-simulator program stay connected to one host through delay, jitter and 2% loss, and reconnect after a drop

items.statement: The in-memory link passes every part of the link script in virtual time, under A0's profile, with a path cut and with a stall. The same seed and the same calls give the same events, and with datagram duplication switched on the script's duplicate check fails.
items.ask: Read the test. Is the link script one piece of code written against the link's interface, which this test and the socket runs both execute? Does the in-memory link take its time from the caller, with no sleep and no wall clock? Under A0's profile does the run report datagrams lost and reordered, each above zero, and reliable messages delayed but never lost? Does the script open a link on which neither game sends and then take the host's reliable message as the first? In its expiry part, does sending stop while the path is still stalled, and is expiry asserted from the sender's counters before the stall ends?

items.statement: On the Mac, over real sockets, a client passes every part of the link script against the host, directly and through the relay under A0's profile. Through the relay the datagram lane loses some and reorders some, and at least 90% of the datagrams sent in the script's lanes and load parts arrive in each direction.
items.ask: Read the harness. Do the client and the host reach the network only through thrum-transport's public interface? Are host, relay and client separate processes, and does the record hold the relay's forwarded and dropped counts and a measured round trip that shows the profile? Is any part of the script skipped, or a failure in it tolerated? In the expiry part, does the record show datagrams expired in the sender's queue, above zero in each direction, apart from the packets the relay dropped?

items.statement: As Wasm in Chrome, over real sockets, a page passes every part of the link script against the host, directly and through the relay under A0's profile, with the same datagram behaviour as the Mac row.
items.ask: Is the page's client thrum-transport's browser adapter running the same link script as Wasm, and not an exchange written in JavaScript? Is Chrome started with no flag that touches certificates, QUIC or origins? Does the record hold the browser's version? In the expiry part, does it say whether the page's queue backed up, and mark what Chrome discards itself as absent and not as zero?

items.statement: In the iPhone simulator, over real sockets, a client passes every part of the link script against the host on the Mac, directly and through the relay under A0's profile, with the same datagram behaviour as the Mac row.
items.ask: Did the client run inside the booted iPhone 18 Pro simulator, built for the simulator target, with the runtime's version and the target triple in the record?

items.statement: One host holds four clients through the relay under A0's profile for ten minutes: two on the Mac, one in Chrome, one in the iPhone simulator. Every link carries the script's load until it closes. In that time a client of each kind closes and reconnects, one is killed, and one path is cut for longer than the idle timeout and then healed. A link still open at the end, once the script stops sending and waits, has delivered every reliable message it accepted, once and in order. A link that an event ended delivered an unbroken run from the first message sent, once and in order, and nothing after it on any link. Every reconnect is a new link.
items.ask: Does the record show each event with its time, the close reason each surviving end reported, and the old and new link identifiers? Is the harness's own note of the kill and the cut kept apart from what the links reported? Did every ended link carry load until its own end reported the close: is the count of reliable messages accepted and never delivered above zero for the cut, and did the host accept messages for the killed client after the kill, so that sends were interrupted and not drained first? Does it name the three kinds of client by platform?

items.statement: With a Mac client, these are on record from two separate runs under A0's profile, each with Cubic and with BBR on the Quinn ends: time from connect to open; datagram and reliable round trips at the median, 95th percentile and maximum, steady and during host-to-client transfers of 256 KiB and 1 MiB; each transfer's time; datagrams delivered; bytes on the wire for each application byte; and the allocations of a warmed send and drain. The record flags each tripwire the design names. The figures are baselines: none decides the result.
items.ask: Were both runs release builds of the claimed commit, timed through thrum-transport and not a stand-in, with the load on the machine recorded? Does the command succeed or fail on the record being complete, and never on a figure?

items.statement: With a Chrome client, the same rows as the Mac's, without allocations, are on record from two separate runs under A0's profile, each with Cubic and with BBR on the host, and with a 256 KiB transfer from the page to the host beside them. What Chrome cannot report is marked absent. The figures are baselines: none decides the result.
No call on a link or a host waits on the network, and the interface names nothing from the libraries beneath it.
items.ask: Can any call on the link's or the host's public interface block, sleep or await? Does that interface name a type from Tokio, Quinn, rustls or wasm-bindgen? Is every queue between the game's side and the I/O side bounded by a cap the link profile sets?

items.statement: The link's interface and the in-memory link build with no outside crate. Only a package that asks for the socket adapters has in its dependency closure a crate this module added to the lockfile, and the V1 game, the starter and the creator scenes have no part of `thrum-transport` in theirs. `thrum-transport`, the proof package and each direct outside dependency are registered with an exact version and a licence.
items.ask: Is every licence in the socket adapters' dependency closure permissive, with none GPL or share-alike? Did the lockfile change the version of any crate that was locked before this module?

items.statement: `./dev check` lints the browser adapter for Wasm, and nothing it runs opens a socket, starts Chrome or calls the simulator.
items.ask: Does `./dev check` run Clippy on thrum-transport's browser adapter for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`? Does any test that `cargo test --workspace` reaches bind or connect a socket?

items.statement: A host's identity is an ECDSA P-256 key and a self-signed certificate valid for less than 14 days, made when the host starts and never written to disk. Every adapter connects only to a host whose certificate has the ticket's SHA-256, and no adapter can be told to skip that check.
items.ask: Read the identity and each adapter's connect path. Is there any option, feature or environment variable that accepts a host without comparing the hash? Is early data (0-RTT) off on both ends? Is the key or certificate ever written to a file or a log?

items.statement: Every registered exact baseline, on the Mac and in Chrome, passes the verifier at the claimed commit: this milestone moved no retained image.

milestones.quality_bar: As dependable as the link under a shipped co-op game. Valve's GameNetworkingSockets gives a game reliable and unreliable messages on one encrypted connection and keeps both moving through packet loss; Factorio's multiplayer notices a dropped peer and takes it back on a fresh connection. Here a link that stays up delivers every reliable message once and in order, no datagram waits behind a lost packet, and a dropped client returns on a new link, proved by one script on all three targets.

milestones.name: A peer that sends garbage, floods, stalls or freezes cannot stop the host or slow the other players, and a game without multiplayer contains no network code

items.statement: The link hello, the length prefix of a reliable message and a ticket's text survive any input: valid input cut at every byte, lengths of zero, the limit, one over and the largest a prefix can say, and random bytes. Each either decodes to exactly what was encoded or is refused, with nothing delivered and no allocation above the lane's cap.
items.ask: Read the test. Does it drive the same decoders the adapters use, with each input kind in the statement generated? Is there a stdin target for each parser, in the style of thrum-network's?

items.statement: Beside three healthy links on real sockets, each of these leaves the host running and the healthy links without a lost or reordered reliable message: random UDP at the port; a wrong ALPN; a wrong WebTransport path; a prefix of zero and one over the limit; a first frame that is not the link hello; a second stream; a datagram over the limit; a stream stalled mid-message; a flood on each lane; more clients than the link cap; handshakes that never finish; clients that connect and never send the hello. A link that broke a rule is closed with that reason and delivers none of the offending bytes.
items.ask: Does the run include every case the statement lists, one at a time? For each, does the record show what the host reported for the offender and the healthy links' reliable counts? Do the host's queued bytes stay within its caps throughout?

items.statement: When one client stops taking messages while the host keeps sending to it, the host's sends to that link return `Full` at the lane's cap, its queued bytes for that link stay within the caps, and three healthy links keep every reliable message in order. Their datagram round trips with and without the stalled link are on record.
items.ask: Does the host in this run make its sends from one thread, as a session's tick would, so that a blocked send to the stalled link would have shown as a stall on the others?

items.statement: A Mac client frozen for longer than the idle timeout: the host reports its link timed out no later than the idle timeout plus one second after the freeze. Resumed, the client reports the link closed, delivers nothing more from it, and opens a new link with the same ticket.
A client in the iPhone simulator frozen for longer than the idle timeout behaves as the Mac's does: timed out at the host, closed on resume, and back on a new link.

A Chrome page closed or reloaded without closing its link is reported closed at the host no later than the idle timeout plus one second, and the page loaded again with the same ticket opens a new link. What the host sees while a page's renderer is frozen for longer than the idle timeout is on record.

The networking design says what is built, and a guide linked from it tells a game maker how to start a host, hand out a ticket, open a link, use each lane within its limits, read events and counters, rehearse on the in-memory link, and run the proof command on the three targets.
items.ask: Do the commands the guide gives run as written at the claimed commit? Does it state both size limits, every close reason, that a ticket dies with its host, that a datagram can arrive long after it was sent, and that a close can cut off the last reliable messages? Does the networking design's transport section still describe anything as selected that this module decided not to build, without saying so?

items.statement: The maturity ledger says what this module proved and what it did not.
items.ask: Do the ledger's N1 and F1 rows keep implementation, correctness and device results apart? Do they name as not run a second machine, any path that is not loopback, a physical iPhone, Safari, Firefox, a public host and the WebSocket fallback, and claim no speed for the simulator?

items.statement: At the closing commit one host again holds two Mac clients, a Chrome page and an iPhone-simulator client for ten minutes through the relay, with M1's events. Again a link still open at the end has delivered every reliable message it accepted, once and in order, and a link that an event ended delivered an unbroken run from the first message sent and nothing after it on any link.

At the closing commit only a package that asks for the socket adapters has in its dependency closure a crate this module added to the lockfile, the V1 game, the starter and the creator scenes have no part of `thrum-transport` in theirs, and the link's interface and in-memory link still build with no outside crate.
Every registered exact baseline, on the Mac and in Chrome, passes the verifier at the claimed commit: this milestone moved no retained image.

milestones.quality_bar: As hard to knock over as the network layer of a public game server. Quinn and Cloudflare's quiche are fuzzed, and a peer's mistake costs that peer its connection and nobody else anything. One hostile, stalled or frozen client costs the host a bounded amount of memory and the other players no reliable message; and, as with Godot's or Unreal's networking, a single-player build carries no socket code.
